_provenance.rules: Plain English, no praise words, figures only where a listed source publishes them, never 'official boundary' (spec §18). Exactly one key fact 'Established YYYY (27 CFR 9.N)', as TTB lists it. Descriptions of 2-4 sentences, at most 700 characters. At most 8 grapes; the 1-3 signature grapes are PRINCIPAL and the rest ACCESSORY. At least two sources per place, one of them the CFR section or the Federal Register final rule. share_pct is left out.

article.description: A small AVA of about 5,774 acres near Los Alamos in northern Santa Barbara County, where the San Antonio Creek valley runs about 20 miles west to the Pacific. At establishment it had nine commercial vineyards on about 238 acres and one winery, and Syrah is its most planted grape.
article.climate: Winkler Region II, about 25 miles from the ocean, in a transition between coast and inland: cool marine air and fog arrive along the San Antonio Creek valley.
article.soils: Mostly sandstone and shale soils of the Paso Robles Formation (63%) and Careaga Sandstone (13%), sandy and quick-draining, with calcium from shale and a rare streak of limestone.
article.grape_varieties: Syrah first, with Grenache, Viognier and Cabernet Franc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Syrah and Grenache, and some Viognier.

article.description: A mountain AVA of about 98,000 acres in the Gabilan Range, across the Monterey–San Benito county line east of the Salinas Valley. It holds the smaller Chalone and Mt. Harlan AVAs. At establishment it had six commercial vineyards, about 436 acres, and four wineries.
article.climate: High and dry: the area averages about 2,370 feet, has fewer than 2.5 hours of fog or cloud a day from June to September (7 to 9 in the areas around it) and about 17 inches of rain a year.
article.soils: Moderately coarse soils over granite bedrock, mainly of the Sheridan-Cieneba-Auberry association, rich in calcium from limestone and quick to drain.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, the grapes of Chalone and Mt. Harlan, which it contains.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from high, limestone-rich sites.

article.description: A small, high AVA of about 7,400 acres in the Gabilan Range in San Benito County, south of Hollister. Its boundary follows the 1,800-foot contour, and its only vineyards are Calera's, planted on limestone, which is rare in California, at an average of about 2,200 feet. Pinot Noir is its main grape.
article.climate: Cooled by the height, about 3 °F for every 1,000 feet, and by Pacific air that reaches it through Monterey Bay; part of the high, dry Gabilan Mountains area, with little summer fog.
article.soils: Limestone-rich soils over granite bedrock in the Gabilan Range.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir first, with Chardonnay and Viognier.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and some Viognier.

article.description: A large AVA that runs almost the whole length of Monterey County, mostly along the Salinas Valley from Monterey Bay south toward the San Luis Obispo County line. It holds Arroyo Seco, Santa Lucia Highlands, Hames Valley, San Bernabe and San Lucas. About 40,000 acres are planted, and Chardonnay is more than half of them.
article.climate: Cool to hot along its roughly 100-mile length: wind and fog from Monterey Bay funnel up the Salinas Valley in the afternoon, so the north is cool and the south warm, with a long growing season and little rain.
article.soils: Loams and sandy loams on the valley floor and benches, from the Chualar and Garey series to Lockwood shaly loam in the south.
article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay over half the vineyard, with Pinot Noir, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and red wines from the warmer south.

article.description: A large inland AVA in northern San Luis Obispo County, about 614,000 acres east of the Santa Lucia Range, with more than 40,000 acres of vines and over 200 wineries. It is split by the Salinas River into a cooler, hillier west side and warmer rolling plains in the east. In 2014 eleven smaller AVAs were established within it.
article.climate: Warm, dry days and cool nights, with some of the widest day-to-night swings in California; marine air reaches the west through the Templeton Gap and other passes in the Santa Lucia Range, while the east is warmer and more continental.
article.soils: Very varied: calcareous shale and limestone-derived soils on the western hills, and alluvial terraces and fans of the Salinas and Estrella rivers in the east.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon is about 39% of the vineyard, then Merlot, Syrah and Zinfandel, with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Petite Sirah and Viognier among many others.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Zinfandel and Rhône varieties, Rhône-style whites and dry rosé.

article.description: The most northwestern of the Paso Robles districts, about 53,100 acres in the southern Santa Lucia Range, with the highest ground in the Paso Robles AVA at about 2,200 feet. Its limestone-rich hills are home to both Rhône and Bordeaux varieties, and Tablas Creek brought Rhône cuttings here.
article.climate: Region II–III with a modest marine influence: cooling winds and fog from Estero Bay to the west, around 25 to 30 inches of rain, and summer swings from about 50 °F at dawn to 95 °F in the afternoon.
article.soils: Shallow residual soils over bedrock from the middle member of the Monterey Formation, largely calcareous, with white chalky rock and limestone.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, with Grenache, Mourvèdre, Zinfandel, Roussanne and other Rhône and Bordeaux varieties.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Rhône and Bordeaux varieties, and Rhône-style whites.

article.description: A district of about 47,000 acres in the southeast of the Paso Robles AVA, on an old erosional plateau at the base of the La Panza Range, drained by Huerhuero Creek. About 1,400 acres are planted, mostly between 1,000 and 1,300 feet, and Bordeaux varieties lead, above all Cabernet Sauvignon.
article.climate: Region III, with about 11.5 inches of rain a year and day-to-night swings of about 25 to 35 °F; Pacific air through the Templeton Gap and cold air draining from the La Panza Range cool it.
article.soils: Old, well-developed terrace and hillside soils from granitic and sedimentary rocks: sandy loams below and clay loams on the terraces and hillsides.
article.grape_varieties: Mostly Bordeaux varieties, above all Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot, Syrah and Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends.

article.soils: Quaternary alluvial soils of different ages on younger and older terraces, from fine sandy loams to clay loams.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot and Petite Sirah, with Sauvignon Blanc, Viognier and Chardonnay.

article.grape_varieties: Bordeaux varieties and Rhône varieties, especially Syrah, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Bordeaux and Rhône varieties.

article.description: The second-largest Paso Robles district, about 60,300 acres in the far southeast, some 33 miles from the ocean, on an old erosional surface from 1,160 to 2,086 feet. article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Syrah, with Zinfandel, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among more than 20 varieties.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Syrah.

article.description: A district of about 35,000 acres in the southwest of the Paso Robles AVA, around Templeton, where gaps in the Santa Lucia Range let cool afternoon air from the Pacific flow inland. article.grape_varieties: Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon, with Syrah and Merlot, and some Pinot Noir and Chardonnay in the coolest spots.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.

article.description: A large AVA around San Francisco Bay, mainly in San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Alameda and Contra Costa counties and partly in Santa Cruz and San Benito. It groups the bay's wine areas, including Livermore Valley, Santa Clara Valley, Lamorinda and the Santa Cruz Mountains, which overlap it. When it was established, nearly 5,800 acres were planted and over 39 wineries operated.

article.wine_styles: Dry red and white wines, from Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel to Chardonnay.

article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay lead, with Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Petite Sirah and Zinfandel; nearly 80% of California's Chardonnay vines trace back to a Livermore Valley clone.
article.wine_styles: Dry reds from Cabernet Sauvignon and Petite Sirah, and dry whites from Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon.

article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay, with Merlot and Zinfandel.

article.description: A coastal AVA of about 408,500 acres along the San Luis Obispo County coast, from coastal terraces and foothills to small valleys that open westward to the Pacific. article.description: A long east–west valley in Santa Barbara County, the Santa Ynez River's, that opens to the Pacific at Lompoc and runs inland past Buellton, Solvang and Los Olivos toward Lake Cachuma. article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah lead, with Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache.

article.description: The largest AVA in Lake County, nearly 220,000 acres around Clear Lake, California's largest natural freshwater lake wholly within the state. Vineyards sit high, from about 1,300 feet at the lakeshore to the slopes of Mount Konocti and beyond. It holds Red Hills Lake County, Big Valley District, Kelsey Bench and Upper Lake Valley.

article.description: A low, rolling AVA at the north shore of San Pablo Bay, spanning the southern ends of Napa and Sonoma counties. It was the first AVA defined by its climate rather than by geography, and it is known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. The name, "the rams", dates from Mexican land grants of the 1830s, and the land was sheep ranches, dairies and hay fields before vines took over in the 1970s.
article.climate: Cool and windy: marine air and fog come straight off San Pablo Bay, summer days rarely pass 80 °F, the difference between day and night is small, and rainfall, at up to about 24 inches, is the lowest in Napa Valley.
article.soils: Shallow, dense clay soils, not very fertile, over a hard claypan that keeps roots near the surface and holds yields down; loams and hillside alluvium in the north.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay above all, with Merlot, Syrah and some Cabernet Sauvignon.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and sparkling wine made from both.

article.description: The main AVA of Mendocino County, north of Sonoma, taking in the inland valleys along the upper Russian River around Ukiah, Hopland and Redwood Valley, and the Anderson Valley toward the coast. It holds Anderson Valley, McDowell Valley, Potter Valley, Redwood Valley and Yorkville Highlands. Much of the county is redwood forest, and vines were first planted here in 1850.

article.soils: Alluvial soils on the valley floors of the Russian River and its tributaries, and older, often red, well-drained soils on the benches and hills.
article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir make up most of the county's crop, followed by Zinfandel, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry whites and reds from Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir and Zinfandel, and sparkling wine from Anderson Valley.

article.description: A narrow valley following the Navarro River northwest toward the Pacific, through Boonville and Philo, in Mendocino County. Its northwest end is only a few miles from the ocean. It grows Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Alsace varieties such as Gewürztraminer and Riesling, and base wine for sparkling wine; about 2,457 acres are planted in some 90 vineyards.

article.soils: Clay on the valley flats and loams over sandstone and shale on the benches and hillsides.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir first, with Chardonnay and the Alsace varieties Gewürztraminer, Riesling and Pinot Gris.

article.description: An AVA made only of coastal ridge-tops in Mendocino County, at or above 1,200 feet, a few miles from the Pacific. The outer boundary encloses about 262,400 acres, but only the 87,466 acres above 1,200 feet count, so the AVA is a scatter of separate hilltops. When it was established there were about 75 acres of vines in six vineyards, many of them Zinfandel.
article.climate: Cool and coastal: the ridge-tops are cooler by day and warmer by night than the valley floors, a difference of about 10 °F, and the grapes keep high natural acidity.
article.soils: Well-drained "timber" soils of sandstone mixed with loamy clay on narrow, forested ridge-tops; the rule judged only about 2% of the land above 1,200 feet suitable for vines.
article.grape_varieties: Zinfandel above all, including old plantings, with some Pinot Noir and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Zinfandel from ridge-top vineyards.

article.description: California's first AVA, a valley about 30 miles long between the Mayacamas Mountains to the west and the Vaca Range to the east, in Napa County. Fifteen smaller AVAs lie within it, from Calistoga at the northern end to Coombsville and Oak Knoll District near the city of Napa, and Los Carneros and Wild Horse Valley overlap its southern edge. It is known above all for Cabernet Sauvignon.
article.climate: A dry Mediterranean climate: warm, rainless summers and mild, wet winters. Fog and wind from San Pablo Bay cool the southern end, and the valley grows warmer toward Calistoga in the north; the mountain AVAs above the fog line see fewer swings between day and night.
article.soils: Very varied over short distances: gravelly and sandy alluvial fans and river deposits on the valley floor, volcanic soils from ash and lava on the eastern side and in the hills, and marine sedimentary soils on the western slopes.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and the other Bordeaux varieties; Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc for whites; Zinfandel and Pinot Noir in smaller amounts.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, dry whites from Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, and sparkling wine from the cooler south.

article.description: A mountain AVA on the western slopes of the Vaca Range, east of the Stags Leap District and the city of Napa, named after the 2,663-foot Atlas Peak. Most of the area lies above 1,400 feet, above much of the valley fog. Wines labelled Atlas Peak must also carry the Napa Valley name.

article.grape_varieties: Mainly Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, above all Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry Chardonnay.

article.description: The northernmost AVA on the Napa Valley floor, around the town of Calistoga below Mount St. Helena, closed in by mountains on three sides. It is the warmest part of the valley floor, and its soils are largely volcanic. Wines labelled Calistoga must also carry the Napa Valley name.

article.description: A long, narrow valley in the Vaca Range in the northeast of Napa County, higher and set apart from the main Napa Valley. It has more vineyards than wineries, and it is named after Joseph Ballinger Chiles, who received a land grant here in 1841. Wines labelled Chiles Valley must also carry the Napa Valley name.

article.description: A horseshoe of hills directly east of the city of Napa, at the foot of the Vaca Range, near the southern end of Napa Valley. It is mostly vineyards, with few wineries, and was known first for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir before Cabernet Sauvignon took over. Wines labelled Coombsville must also carry the Napa Valley name.

article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Merlot, with Pinot Noir and Syrah.

article.description: A hillside AVA of about 4,000 acres on the western face of the Vaca Range, east of St. Helena and south of Howell Mountain. It covers slopes between 400 and 1,400 feet, with no flat ground, and about 230 acres of vineyard in some 30 commercial vineyards when it was established in 2024. It was Napa Valley's first new AVA in 13 years.

article.soils: Thin, well-drained volcanic soils, with volcanic ash on slopes of 15 to 40 percent.
article.grape_varieties: Mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, planted on the hillside vineyards.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, chiefly Cabernet Sauvignon.

article.description: A mountain AVA in the Mayacamas range just south of Calistoga, at the northwest end of Napa Valley. Its name comes from shards of volcanic glass in the soil. Jacob Schram planted vines here in 1862. Wines labelled Diamond Mountain District must also carry the Napa Valley name.

article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates, with Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, chiefly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends.

article.description: A plateau in the Vaca Range above St. Helena, around the village of Angwin, and the first AVA established inside Napa Valley. article.soils: Decomposed granite, rocky and sandy loams.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted, with Syrah, Chardonnay, Merlot, and Mediterranean varieties such as Sangiovese, Tempranillo and Viognier.
article.wine_styles: Dry reds from Bordeaux and Mediterranean varieties, dry whites and rosé.
key_facts: Established 1984 (27 CFR 9.50)
